newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to complete checklist on its future.
newsitem.headline: EU to complete checklist on its future.

text.p: Like students taking an exam, European Union countries will be asked this week to check boxes saying just how much Qualified Majority Voting they are prepared to live with.

In a move to force the pace of inter-governmental conference (IGC) negotiations, Ireland has asked its partners to explain in which circumstances they would be willing to cede unanimity in favour of QMV.
The EU presidency has handed each country a five-page checklist to gauge where they may be willing to bend.

Foreign ministers' representatives, meeting in Brussels on Monday and Tuesday, will be asked to tick boxes marked "yes", "no" or "willing to consider further" next to some 50 treaty articles where unanimity is currently required for EU decisions.

They will also be asked to consider giving more co-decision power to the European Parliament in areas ranging from citizens' rights to development aid, and to consider possible changes to the way the European Court of Justice operates.
The issues on the agenda are particularly sensitive in Britain, where the ruling Conservative Party is torn over the country's future in Europe.
London has vowed to fight any move to extend QMV, is generally sceptical about giving the parliament more power and wants some of the court's powers to be curbed.

But sharp differences also exist in other EU countries. Many, while agreeing that more QMV or some variation of it is needed for an enlarged bloc to work efficiently, object to losing unanimity in specific areas such as tax and Common Foreign and Security Policy.
They also differ over the desirability of promoting the parliament. France, for example, has little time for the body, while Germany considers it an essential element in EU democracy.
In an introductory note for the meeting, the Irish said the checklist was necessary because there was no agreement on an overall approach to decision making.

"The application of certain criteria for use of QMV is favoured by some member states and this would contribute to a coherent approach," it said. "However, none of the criteria considered to date seems likely to receive unanimous support.
"It appears, therefore, that a case-by-case examination will be necessary to define areas where a move could be made from unanimity to a qualified-majority vote," it said.

Most EU decisions are already taken by qualified majority, but certain key areas -- taxation, foreign policy and some economic areas such as agreements on an exchange-rate system -- still require a unanimous vote.
The negotiators will also consider whether to give the parliament more co-decision powers.
The assembly was given a limited right to block legislation in the Maastricht treaty and some think that should be extended.

In its note, the presidency conceded there was no consensus, but asked negotiators to consider a report by the European Commission recommending that the parliament be given broader co-decision powers.

The Commission lists a number of areas where that would be appropriate, including measures concerning non-discrimination, citizenship, the internal market, indirect taxation, structural funds and staff regulations.
However, it specifically rules out co-decision in constitutional areas, economic and monetary union and most trade areas.

The Irish note said there was widespread agreement that the Court of Justice should have at least one judge from each country and that some had suggested creating two separate chambers -- if it could be done without damaging the court.

The note said some countries had also argued that access to the court should be broadened for individuals, the parliament, the Court of Auditors, the Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions.

But it said one delegation -- presumably Britain, which has spoken publicly on the issue -- wanted the court to be given the power to limit the retrospective effect of its judgments and to limit damages to cases of "grave and manifest infringement" of Community law.
The negotiators will also consider a number of issues raised by the Union's future enlargement. These include weighting of votes in the Council of Ministers and the size of the Commission.
All these are set to be discussed on Monday and Tuesday, but only the question of QMV is being forced by the distribution of the checklist.
